scimon.text: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Mn0.6Ni1−xSi0.62Fe0.4CoxGe0.38 high-entropy alloys with x = 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, and 0.55; after annealing and quenching, the alloys were predominantly hexagonal Ni2In-type at 295 K, with x = 0.40 containing 98.6% Ni2In-type and 1.4% orthorhombic TiNiSi-type phase and the higher-x alloys reported as 100% Ni2In-type.
hidden_target.intervention: Systematically substituted Co for Ni by increasing x from 0.40 to 0.55, while characterizing structure, magnetostructural transitions, magnetocaloric response, and mechanical properties. Alloys were arc-melted under Ar from >99.99 wt.% elements with 5 at.% excess Mn, annealed at 750 °C for 72 h in high vacuum, and water-quenched.
hidden_target.conditions: Structures were measured at 295 K by Cu Kα XRD/Rietveld refinement; DSC was performed from 183–400 K at 10 K min−1 under N2; thermomagnetic measurements used 0.05 T, and isothermal magnetization/entropy measurements used fields up to 5 T near TC. Direct ΔTad was measured with 120 s in-field residence, 180 mm s−1 sample motion, and 0.5 K min−1 heating under a 5 T superconducting field and a 4.8 T pulsed field. Hardness used a 2 kg load for 10 s.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Increasing Co raised the hexagonal lattice ratio chex/ahex slightly (about 1.290 to 1.291), strengthened/stabilized the high-temperature hexagonal Ni2In-type phase, shifted the hexagonal-to-orthorhombic TiNiSi-type transformation downward, and ultimately changed the transition from coupled first-order magnetostructural behavior for x = 0.40–0.50 to a second-order magnetic transition for x = 0.55.
hidden_target.mechanism: Co-for-Ni substitution was attributed to strengthening covalent bonding between neighboring Mn atoms, stabilizing the Ni2In-type austenite and lowering the structural-transition and Curie temperatures. When the structural transition lies near TC, coupling between ferromagnetic TiNiSi-type martensite and paramagnetic Ni2In-type austenite produces latent heat, hysteresis, and a giant magnetocaloric response; loss of this coupling at x = 0.55 yields a small second-order response. Reduced lattice distortion/internal stress at the second-order transition was also associated with improved mechanical properties.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to the low-Co x = 0.40 alloy, increasing Co substitution was found to progressively lower Ttr, TC, and peak magnetic entropy change, eventually suppressing the giant first-order magnetocaloric effect at x = 0.55, while generally increasing hardness and giving the highest compressive strength at x = 0.55.
hidden_target.baseline: The principal compositional baseline was x = 0.40, the Ni-richer alloy with room-temperature magnetostructural coupling and the largest magnetocaloric response; Gd was additionally used as a reference for direct ΔTad measurements.
hidden_target.boundary: The giant response holds for x = 0.40–0.50 where first-order magnetostructural coupling occurs near TC; x = 0.55 instead shows a second-order transition and small MCE, with its structural transition outside the DSC range of 183–400 K. The strongest room-temperature performance occurs for x = 0.40 around 306–309 K and fields up to 5 T.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: XRD/Rietveld phase fractions and lattice ratios; DSC peaks, latent heat, and entropy; heating/cooling M(T) curves and thermal hysteresis; isothermal M(H)-derived −ΔSM via the Maxwell relation; field-scaling exponent n, where nmax > 2 identifies first-order and nmax < 2 second-order behavior; and direct ΔTad measurements under superconducting and pulsed fields.
hidden_target.actual_result: Ttr decreased from 306 K (x = 0.40) to 286 K (0.45) and 269 K (0.50), while no DSC peak was observed for x = 0.55 within 183–400 K. TC values were 309, 289, 272, and 259 K, with thermal hysteresis of 21, 20, 24, and 12 K, respectively. At 5 T, peak −ΔSM decreased from 48.5 to 42.9, 31.7, and 2.6 J kg−1 K−1 as x increased. For x = 0.40, direct ΔTad peaked at 8.2 K near 306.5 K under 5 T and 14.1 K under a 4.8 T pulsed field; the abstract instead reports 8.6 K at 306.5 K. DSC entropy changes for x = 0.40, 0.45, and 0.50 were 56.4, 27.3, and 24.8 J kg−1 K−1. The n criterion confirmed first-order transitions for x = 0.40–0.50 and a second-order transition for x = 0.55. Reported hardness values across increasing x were 552, 677, 683, and 758 HV2, and compressive strengths were 78, 21, 117, and 267 MPa; the abstract inconsistently assigns 552 HV2 to x = 0.55.
